title: The Angle of the Door Determines Survival
sensory_anchor: her bedroom door — the angle it opens determines whether she can see the hallway
emotional_signature: geometry as survival: the angle is the variable
body: Her bedroom door opens inward. The hinge is on the left. When it opens, it reveals the hallway to the right. She cannot see the left side of the hallway from her bed. She positions her pillow so she can see the door's angle without sitting up. A door that opens 30 degrees means someone is looking in. A door that opens 90 degrees means someone is coming in. A door that opens slowly means he is measuring her response. A door that opens fast means he has already decided. The angle of the door is not decoration. It is information. She reads angles the way other people read faces. The geometry of the door — its hinge placement, its swing radius, the sight lines it creates or destroys — is load-bearing. A door that opens the wrong way is a design flaw that can kill you.

title: Sight Lines and Approach Vectors
sensory_anchor: the approach to the meeting point — she maps the angles before she walks
emotional_signature: operational geometry: approach from the blind side, exit at the obtuse angle
body: The meeting is in a cafe. Corner table. The target faces the door. She approaches from the side entrance, the one he cannot see from his seat. She does not think 'approach vector.' She thinks: the angle. The geometry of approach matters. Coming from the front gives him time to compose. Coming from the side gives her the first read. The stepfather's house taught her this: the angle of approach determines who sees whom first. The grandmother's kitchen taught her the complement: approach from the direction where you are expected, and the encounter is comfortable. She uses both. With targets, she approaches from the blind angle. With allies, she approaches from the expected one. The geometry of approach is not strategy. It is instinct.

title: Load-Bearing vs Decorative
sensory_anchor: the organizational chart — she reads it as a structural diagram, not a hierarchy
emotional_signature: the same question: what holds this up, and what is just surface?
body: The target's organization has a hierarchy on paper and a structure in reality. The hierarchy is decorative. The structure is load-bearing. The VP of Operations reports to the CEO on paper, but the real authority runs through the logistics manager who controls the supply chain. She reads the structure the way she reads a building: what supports what? Where is the load-bearing wall? Where is the decorative facade? The stepfather's house had a decorative hierarchy (her mother was nominally in charge of the household) and a load-bearing structure (he controlled everything). She learned to read past the facade before she was ten. In organizations, the same skill applies. The org chart is the facade. The actual flow of authority is the structure. Remove the load-bearing element and the structure collapses. Remove the decorative element and nothing changes.

title: Relationships Have Angles
sensory_anchor: the protectee and his friend — the angle between them tells her the state of the friendship
emotional_signature: reading social geometry the same way she reads physical geometry
body: The protectee and his friend are sitting on the couch. The angle between them is open — they face each other, shoulders aligned, lean forward. This is a stable geometry. A week ago, the angle was closed — they sat parallel, not facing, a gap between them. She reads the angle the same way she reads a room. Relationships have geometry. The angle between two people — how they sit, how they stand, how they walk together — tells her more than their words do. The stepfather and her mother sat at right angles: she facing him, he facing the television. The grandmother and the child sat facing each other across the table. The geometry of a relationship is not metaphorical. It is physical. It is information.
